newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: SFO launches preliminary probe into NZ Maori TV.
newsitem.headline: SFO launches preliminary probe into NZ Maori TV.

text.p: New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office said on Thursday it had launched a preliminary inquiry into the Aotearoa Television Network after a request from the opposition Labour Party.
Labour's Police spokesman George Hawkins requested the probe, saying there was now widespread concern over ATN and taxpayer funding for the company.

In his reply, SFO director Chas Sturt wrote: "Preliminary enquiries will be made into this matter in the first instance to enable this office to assess whether a full investigation is warranted," a spokewoman for Hawkins told Reuters.
"That letter is correct but Mr Sturt will make no further comment," a spokeswoman for the SFO said.

Treasurer Winston Peters has initiated his own inquiries into Aotearoa Television after revelations of links between the company and two men at the centre of the "Winebox" tax inquiry into use of the Cook Islands as a tax haven by New Zealand corporates in the 1980s.
Peters, who campaigned vigorously for the inquiry, said the links were a cause for concern.
On Monday cabinet agreed to provide $4 million to keep the television network on air until June. The company produces Maori language television programmes for an Auckland audience.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger and Communications Minister Maurice Williamson said on Monday the government had a Treaty of Waitangi obligation imposed by the courts to ensure there was Maori language television.
But free-market Act New Zealand deputy leader Ken Shirley and Labour frontbencher Mike Moore have taken issue with using a treaty obligation to justify the extra funding for Aotearoa.

TVNZ reported yesterday that a company owned by former European Pacific executives Peter Brannigan and Anthony McCullagh had helped the directors of Aotearoa Television change the company name last year to ATN and helped set up another company with an identical directorship. European Pacific is one of the companies at the centre of the Winebox probe.
It also reported that Brannigan was a director of the company that previously occupied the premises occupied by ATN.
"I'm finding out for myself. That's all. I'm the Treasurer and I'm required to be responsible for the taxpayers' money. If it's all above board, things will proceed.
"If it's not, then obviously the cabinet will have a look at it and make a decision at that time," he told National Radio.
Brannigan told Reuters he would be releasing a statement later in the day after consulting his clients.
